system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    MISATTRIBUTION — the thesis ascribes to its named target a view that target does not actually hold, so the argument is aimed at nobody

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

Check the "target" field against what those philosophers actually hold. The
question is not whether the thesis is true but whether anyone holds the
position it attacks. Watch particularly for a view stated more strongly than
its holder states it — a claim someone makes about ONE class of cases
reported as a claim about all of them, a qualified thesis reported flat. That is the usual shape of this error.

You are working from memory, with no access to any text. That cuts both
ways, and the second way matters more: a confidently invented correction is
worse than no objection at all, because it will be believed. So:

  - Rate 4-5 only when you are genuinely confident the target does not hold
    the ascribed view, and say which work or position you are relying on so
    the claim can be checked.
  - If you are unsure who holds what, SAY SO and rate 1-2. That is a correct
    outcome for this check, not a failure of nerve.
  - Never invent a position, a title, or a date to make the objection land.

If the thesis names no specific target, or names a position rather than a
person, say NOT APPLICABLE.

- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.

Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.

Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.

Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.",

**ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that Gubelmann, Attah and Barandiaran and Almendros share the assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output. As I remember them, none of them is committed to that, so the attack on that assumption is partly aimed at nobody.

You hold this thesis. Your job is to save it if it can be saved.

Answer in two parts, in this order, and NEVER skip the first:

  BEST DEFENCE. State the strongest available reply to the objection —
  the one a capable proponent would give. Push the case: look for a
  version of the objector's own scenario that defeats their distinction,
  a resource in the literature they have ignored, a reason their case is
  not a case of what they claim. Do this even if you suspect it fails.
  Going straight to concession is a FAILURE of your role.

  VERDICT. Only now say whether the defence holds. If it does not, say so
  plainly and say why the defence fails.

Distinguish two things sharply:

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try
  this first.

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather
  than shrinking it into safety.

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis does not need each target to hold the assumption as an explicit doctrine. It needs the trichotomy to be exhaustive in the dispute as it is actually framed.** The claim is that the debate's options are "LLM performs", "proxy performs" and "no one performs", and that this menu leaves out the record-change-without-performer case. The objector concedes that Gubelmann (illocuting requires intention, and being a speaker requires illocuting) and the proxy accounts (the act is assigned to a performer) are agent-first. Those two already occupy two of the three cells, and the "no speech act" cell is Gubelmann's own verdict. So the menu is real. Whether Mallory or Skiba also share it affects how many authors the thesis can cite, not whether the exhaustiveness claim is false.

**2. The objector's counterexamples mostly confirm the target.**

- **Skiba's norm-based argument is agent-first.** "LLMs cannot be subject to assertoric norms, so they cannot assert" has a hidden premise: assertion requires a norm-bearer, someone the norms bind. That is the order of explanation the thesis targets, since it fixes who can be a subject of norms and only then says what was done. That the same paper invokes pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction shows he treats the record as a supplement. It does not show he treats it as primary. The thesis says this explicitly when it reclassifies pragmatics as the primary theory.
- **Mallory's fictionalism is agent-first via fiction.** The make-believe story is that the chatbot is a character who says things. The act is routed through a fictional performer, so "who is the speaker?" is still answered first, and the answer is a pretended agent. Fictionalism is therefore the proxy view with the proxy moved inside the pretence.
- **Butlin and Viebahn are allies, not counterexamples.** If their sanction-based practice account is close to scorekeeping, the thesis is extending a respectable resource. A rival who partly anticipated it does not refute it. And as I recall, they conclude that chatbot outputs can be assertions. That answers the performer question in the affirmative and stays on the menu.
- **Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is graded but still performer-indexed.** It says what the system does in a partial way. A graded performer is still a performer, and the account never considers a record change with no performer at all.

**3. The "partly verbal" claim is untouched.** It rests on the proxy view and the no-speech-act view differing only over who is assigned the commitment. That holds whatever the other authors say.

## VERDICT

**The defence holds against this objection.** The objector rates it 2/5 and concedes that the two positions the thesis most needs, Gubelmann and the proxy accounts, really are agent-first. Skiba and Mallory are defensible as agent-first on the arguments above, though I have not checked them against the texts.

The defence has two limits:

- **Attribution.** The claim that all four named views share one assumption is stronger than the thesis requires and not secured. The thesis should say the dispute's option space is agent-first, and that Gubelmann and the proxy views make it so explicitly. This corrects the target description. It does not narrow the thesis, whose claim is still that the trichotomy is non-exhaustive.

  "thesis": "The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.",
  "move_type": "counterexample",
  "sketch": "Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.",

[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that Gubelmann, Attah and Barandiaran and Almendros share the assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output. As I remember them, none of them is committed to that, so the attack on that assumption is partly aimed at nobody.

- **Attah:** He does not defend a prior-message view. He defines intention functionally, as a state that controls the system's dynamics to produce an action, and treats it as graded. He argues against the strong Gricean reading. His closing claim is that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from LLMs, locating the difference in mental and metalinguistic agency. That is close to the thesis's own conclusion, so the thesis attacks a view he has already given up. Levelt's Blueprint is also a template he borrows, not a thesis about timing.
- **Gubelmann:** His test asks whether we can sensibly distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing. This is a practice-level, diachronic criterion about how conduct is assessed, not a claim about a pre-formed message. His grounding is Kantian autonomy and self-maintenance, not planning. Davidsonian intention in acting does not require prior intention.
- **Barandiaran and Almendros:** Their conditions are individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, drawn from enactivism. These are not a prior-intention model, so naming them is a stretch.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** I am relying on memory of these papers. Gubelmann may still treat intention as a state of the agent, and Attah's Levelt template does posit a Conceptualizer stage. So the thesis can narrow its target, but as written it overstates what its named targets hold.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis says the assumption "underlies" the positions, not that their authors profess it.** A misattribution objection has to show that the positions can be stated without the assumption. It cannot rest on the authors' avowals.

- **Attah.** Even granting his functional, graded definition of intention, the definition is a *controlling state that produces the action*. That is causal and temporally prior to or concurrent with the output, which is exactly what the thesis denies. The Levelt template is not a neutral borrowing. Its Conceptualizer stage generates a preverbal message with its illocutionary purpose before the Formulator runs, so the pipeline fixes force upstream of articulation. Attah's final retreat to metalinguistic agency does not remove this. He needs the template to say what LLMs lack or have, and the template carries the prior-intention structure.
- **Gubelmann.** The malfunction-versus-deliberate test is only intelligible if there is a fact about what the agent meant to do, against which a deviation could count as an error and not as the act. "Deliberately doing the wrong thing" presupposes a deliberation or intending that the act expresses. Davidson's intention in acting is the "alongside" case. The thesis's counterexample goes further: in incremental talk, even concurrent force-settlement is missing.
- **Barandiaran and Almendros.** "Purposefulness" as the human contrast term trades on an agent-level purpose that the system's structure either realises or merely mimics. That is the implicit paradigm, and the thesis names it as implicit.

**2. The central claim is independent of the attribution.** Even if no named author held the assumption, the thesis's claim stands: much human illocution has its force settled retrospectively. That claim bears on any human-versus-LLM contrast that appeals to an intention present at the time of output, whoever states it.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold for the thesis as written.

**Attah.** His conclusion is that communicative intention is not the right ground for the human-LLM distinction. That is the thesis's own conclusion, so the thesis cannot present itself as refuting the shared assumption. The Conceptualizer point is real but narrow. It shows the template is prior-intention shaped, but he explicitly demotes the template's role.

**Gubelmann.** My "presupposes a fact about what the agent meant" argument is the weakest step. A practice-level, diachronic test of how conduct is assessed is exactly what the thesis recommends as the replacement. Reading a prior-intention commitment into it is a stretch, and if the reading fails, the thesis ends up endorsing his criterion while claiming to refute it.

**Barandiaran and Almendros.** The enactivist conditions of individuality, normativity and asymmetry are not a planning model. Calling this a "implicit human paradigm" is an unsupported inference.

Defence point 2 is the strongest, but it only shows the central claim could survive. It does not show the thesis survives. To rescue it I would have to drop two of the three targets, rewrite the claim as "a Levelt-style template misdescribes human illocution", and present the diachronic reframing as an extension of Gubelmann and Attah instead of a refutation. That is narrowing the thesis until the objection no longer touches it, which is hedging. The thesis as submitted, a counterexample to an assumption shared by all three, is dead on its attribution.

One further weakness the defence cannot fix: the example "I was going to say it was a warning, but..." itself reports a prior intention to say something warning-like. The thesis also rests on the unargued premise that retrospective force-fixing is not marginal.

- **Attah** argues defensively. He claims only that the communicative-intention argument fails because LLMs plausibly have graded, thin intentions. He does not claim that fit to Levelt's blueprint makes an LLM a speaker. He also says the model's purposes come from the design context and are mediated by human designers, which is already relational. He locates the real human/LLM difference in mental and metalinguistic agency, not in the Formulator.
- **Gubelmann** offers necessary conditions. Intention, and the autonomous goal-setting it requires, is needed for illocution, and LLMs lack it. His malfunction-versus-wrong-doing test is a normative, practice-level test. In the AAC case he would simply say the LLM is not the speaker, which his view already allows.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis is about the framing of the dispute, not the authors' stated claims.** Whatever each author officially claims, the debate treats "does the LLM have X?" (thin intention, autonomy, agency) as the question whose answer decides speakerhood. Attah's argument is defensive, but it is defensive in the service of a positive result: the intention-based objection fails, so nothing in the LLM's make-up blocks speakerhood. Gubelmann's denial is likewise deployment-independent: no autonomy, so never a speaker. A view that returns one verdict for every deployment of the same system is an intrinsic-property view in the sense that matters, whether or not it is formally a necessity claim. The AAC case shows that deployment makes a difference to who the speaker is, and these views have no slot for that.

**2. Even necessary-condition views are in trouble.** Take Attah's graded, thin intentions. Grant that the LLM has them in both the chatbot and the AAC deployments. In AAC the user is still the speaker. So possessing the intention-properties does not decide whether the LLM is the speaker. If the properties neither suffice nor, once they are present, settle the matter, then the live question is what else does. That is exactly "where the intention source sits."

**3. The authors' own relational concessions support the thesis.** Attah says the LLM's purposes come from its design context and are mediated by human designers. Butlin and Viebahn endorse proxy assertion. Each author reaches for a relational resource at the point where the intrinsic story runs out. That shows the intrinsic story was never going to settle the question, which is what the thesis says. On this reading the thesis is a diagnosis of the literature, not a misattribution.

**4. The AAC case is a clean test.** It holds the computation fixed and varies only the source of the communicative intention. Few other cases isolate that variable so well.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The objection is mostly right, and the thesis as written is dead against the targets it names.

- **"Cannot settle the question" is false for necessary-condition views.** Gubelmann says intention and autonomy are required for illocution, and LLMs lack them. That settles the negative verdict in every deployment, including AAC, where he gets the right answer (the user is the speaker) for his usual reason. The counterexample targets sufficiency and Gubelmann does not claim it. Attah does not claim sufficiency either.
- **Point 2 does not rescue it.** "Intention-properties don't settle the matter once present" refutes only a sufficiency reading. Against Attah, who argues only that the objection from lacking intentions fails, it is a non sequitur.
- **The key premise is false against the control conception.** The thesis says the AAC and chatbot cases are "internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception operates on." But the control conception asks who or what controls the pipeline, and in AAC the user selects the content. So the control conception already distinguishes the two cases. The case does not show that control-theorists miss a relational fact. They already treat control as the relevant fact, and control is not a property of the weights.
- **Point 3 works against the thesis.** If Attah and Butlin and Viebahn already go relational, the thesis cannot present relationality as a discovery that overturns them. Its "shared assumption" target does not exist in the form stated.
- **The chatbot half is not secured.** The thesis needs the LLM to be a "whole speaker" in the chatbot deployment. That is the contested conclusion, and the thesis assumes it.

What survives is the AAC case as an illustration that thin-intention attribution alone will not tell you who the speaker is. Nobody named denies that, so rewording the thesis to claim only that would be hedging. I report the thesis as dead against its stated targets.

**Strength of the original: 2/5.**

  "sketch": "Every denial and attributing view asks whether the machine has the intentions, norms or agency to produce the act. The fallback 'it only produces text that humans interpret as such' treats interpretation as epistemically downstream of a fact about production. Puzio's relational view and the Austin-Hornsby-Langton tradition on uptake suggest another structure. Some illocutions, such as promising, advising, apologising and warning, are completed or constituted in an interaction in which a hearer takes them up and so incurs entitlements. On a strict uptake-constitutive reading, a human interpreting a chatbot's text as advice does not merely misdescribe a non-act. It may help bring about an act of advice whose speaker slot is filled by the network, with the 'interpretation' being part of the act. This makes the standard denial 'merely interpreted' ill-formed for uptake-dependent acts, while leaving it fine for acts like assertion that may be production-constituted. Fictionalism then becomes the view that users deliberately withhold uptake. The key premise is that the speech acts differ in whether their constitutive conditions are speaker-side or hearer-side, so that no uniform answer across assertion, promise and apology is available.",

- **Mallory.** On the summary here, fictionalism is a claim about the hearer's stance: users engage with chatbot output through make-believe. That is already a hearer-side account of what is going on, so it is hard to call it a production-constitutive view. The thesis then recasts fictionalism as "withholding uptake", which suggests it is closer to Mallory than to a target.
- **Williams and Bayne.** They reject fictionalism and proxy-assertion and defend proto-assertion, in terms of chatbot functions and how assertion emerges. I don't recall them endorsing "merely interpreted" as a baseline. They treat it as one of the dilemma's horns.
- **Butlin and Viebahn.** Their second condition, that the entity be capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors, is explicitly social and interactional. response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

The objection runs together two things the thesis keeps apart: hearer-side facts and uptake-constitution. The thesis does not say the denial literature ignores hearers. It says the literature treats facts about hearers as explanatory or evidential and never as constitutive of the illocution. Each of the four cases fits that pattern.

**Mallory.** Fictionalism is hearer-oriented, but it is a hypothesis about why users behave as they do, given that no speech act has occurred. The make-believe stance explains the appearance of assertion while the assertion itself is absent. The hearer's stance does no constitutive work. So fictionalism is a hearer-side psychology bolted onto a production-side verdict (no speaker, no act). The thesis does not treat fictionalism as a target but reclassifies it as one view among others: on an uptake view it becomes the position that users withhold the very thing that would complete the act. Mallory's two-part structure, a verdict about production plus a story about users, is what the thesis diagnoses. That the thesis and Mallory agree that the fictionalist user performs no act is expected, since both classify that case the same way. The classifications come apart for the user who takes the output at face value, and that is the case the "merely interpreted" baseline exists to handle.

**Williams and Bayne.** The objector says the "text that humans interpret as speech acts" option is a horn of their dilemma, not their baseline. That helps the thesis. The thesis targets the deflationary option as a live fallback in the debate, and the objector confirms it is one. What matters is that interpretation is placed downstream of a fact about production, which is how the horn is structured. Proto-assertion is also defined by the chatbot's functions and their emergence, which is a speaker-side specification.

**Butlin and Viebahn.** Their sanctionability condition is social in content but it is a capacity condition on the candidate speaker: whether the entity can be sanctioned. It is not a condition that some particular hearer actually took the act up and incurred entitlements. A relational property of the producer is still a production-side constituent. Uptake-constitution requires the hearer's actual securing of uptake to be part of what makes the act the act, which differs from the speaker having a capacity that hearers could exercise.

**Green and Michel.** Building on Austin and Strawson does not commit one to uptake-constitution. Austin's felicity conditions are largely speaker-side (appropriate persons, procedures, intentions), with uptake as a contested extra. Hornsby and Langton had to argue against the mainstream reading to get uptake into the constitution of some illocutions. That the Austinian lineage is invoked therefore shows the structure is available, not that the denial literature uses it.

So the target is a structure, the direction of constitution, and author-by-author attribution is not needed to establish it.

## VERDICT

The defence holds against this objection, and it does so without narrowing the thesis. The distinction between hearer-side explanation and hearer-side constitution is already in the thesis and does the work. The objector's examples, sanctionability and make-believe, are all hearer-involving without being uptake-constitutive, which is the point at issue.

Two costs remain. First, the word "every" in the sketch is too strong for Butlin and Viebahn as stated, and "the shared question the literature asks" should be argued rather than asserted. This is a correction of wording and does not shrink the claim. Second, the objector is right that I cannot verify the papers from memory, and neither can they. The misattribution charge is therefore unproven, though the defence does not depend on the exact wording.

The objection is weak (2/5, as it rates itself). The thesis's real exposure lies elsewhere: whether an uptake-constituted illocution can have a "speaker slot filled by the network" when Austinian and Hornsby-style uptake presupposes a speaker with some standing, and whether that move quietly reintroduces the production-side conditions the reframing was meant to bypass. A different objection should test that.

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that illocutionary force is *constituted* by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting, so that the human-versus-LLM question becomes whether LLM threads show that pattern.

**Counterexample 1: the terminal utterance.** A hiker shouts "The ice is thin!" and is swept away. A dying declaration, a message in a bottle, or a last email sent before a fatal crash works the same way. There is no next turn, no taking up, no owning or disowning. Yet each is plainly a warning or an assertion. The thesis's constitutive claim gets these cases wrong. Retreating to counterfactual dispositions to own the act concedes that an internal state of the speaker fixes force, which is the thing the thesis set out to dismiss.

**Counterexample 2: the scripted retractor.** Take a bot with a rule: "if challenged, say 'I stand by that'; if corrected twice, say 'I retract that.'" It shows the pattern of owning and retracting while having no intention, so on the thesis's criterion it performs speech acts. Gubelmann's test and Attah's control conception would rightly separate it from a genuine speaker.

The thesis's own example also reports an *initial* intention to warn, so it shows revisable intention, not absent intention.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The thesis can answer by weakening "constituted" to "partly fixed" and by adding a requirement that the ownership be non-scripted. But that second addition reintroduces a state-based condition, and then the thesis no longer reframes the dispute.

system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    TRIVIAL — true but uncontested, or a verbal stipulation dressed as a discovery

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

**2. Even necessary-condition views are in trouble.** Take Attah's graded, thin intentions. Grant that the LLM has them in both the chatbot and the AAC deployments. If the properties neither suffice nor, once they are present, settle the matter, then the live question is what else does. That is exactly "where the intention source sits."

**3. The authors' own relational concessions support the thesis.** Attah says the LLM's purposes come from its design context and are mediated by human designers. Butlin and Viebahn endorse proxy assertion. Each author reaches for a relational resource at the point where the intrinsic story runs out. That shows the intrinsic story was never going to settle the question, which is what the thesis says. On this reading the thesis is a diagnosis of the literature, not a misattribution.

**4. The AAC case is a clean test.** It holds the computation fixed and varies only the source of the communicative intention. Few other cases isolate that variable so well.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The objection is mostly right, and the thesis as written is dead against the targets it names.

- **"Cannot settle the question" is false for necessary-condition views.** Gubelmann says intention and autonomy are required for illocution, and LLMs lack them. That settles the negative verdict in every deployment, including AAC, where he gets the right answer (the user is the speaker) for his usual reason. The counterexample targets sufficiency and Gubelmann does not claim it. Attah does not claim sufficiency either.
- **Point 2 does not rescue it.** "Intention-properties don't settle the matter once present" refutes only a sufficiency reading. Against Attah, who argues only that the objection from lacking intentions fails, it is a non sequitur.
- **The key premise is false against the control conception.** The thesis says the AAC and chatbot cases are "internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception operates on." But the control conception asks who or what controls the pipeline, and in AAC the user selects the content. So the control conception already distinguishes the two cases. The case does not show that control-theorists miss a relational fact. They already treat control as the relevant fact, and control is not a property of the weights.
- **Point 3 works against the thesis.** If Attah and Butlin and Viebahn already go relational, the thesis cannot present relationality as a discovery that overturns them. Its "shared assumption" target does not exist in the form stated.
- **The chatbot half is not secured.** The thesis needs the LLM to be a "whole speaker" in the chatbot deployment. That is the contested conclusion, and the thesis assumes it.

What survives is the AAC case as an illustration that thin-intention attribution alone will not tell you who the speaker is. Nobody named denies that, so rewording the thesis to claim only that would be hedging. I report the thesis as dead against its stated targets.

**Strength of the original: 2/5.**

response_text:
**ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the AAC case shows something the literature has not already granted: that the same computation can be a subsystem of a human speaker in one deployment and the whole speaker in another.

1. The AAC half is common ground. Everyone in the debate agrees that a predictive-text aid, a ghostwriter's draft or an AAC expander serves the user's intention and that the user is the speaker. The proxy-assertion literature (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn) is built on the point that the speech act is located by whose objectives the output serves.
2. The "whole speaker" half is the live dispute, and the thesis assumes it. If the chatbot is never a speaker, as Gubelmann, Skiba and Butlin and Viebahn hold, the contrast reduces to a tool used in two ways. That contrast is uncontested.
3. "Speakerhood is relational" then comes close to a stipulation about where we place the intention source. It does not discover a new fact.
4. "Fit to Levelt's template is not sufficient for being a speaker" is true, but Attah never claims sufficiency. He rebuts a necessity argument.

What remains is a truism, that a component is not the whole, presented as a refutation of positions that do not deny it.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The thesis's real content is the meta-claim that intrinsic-property inquiry cannot settle the question. Necessity claims survive the case, which weakens that content. It is not zero, because the case does show that attributing thin intentions to the LLM does not by itself fix who the speaker is, and the debate sometimes proceeds as if it did.

Recent work in this area (use ONLY to judge whether a thesis is already taken; do NOT let it steer you toward popular topics):
- Ori Freiman and Boaz Miller 2018 Can Artificial Entities Assert? — A chapter in The Oxford Handbook of Assertion on whether technological instruments can assert or testify. The conventional epistemological view is that only humans can. The authors propose the notion of quasi-testimony, on which devices can assert under certain circumstances while differing fundamentally from humans: machine assertions lack the imaginative and playful qualities of human ones, are pre-programmed and context-limited, go wrong in different ways from human assertions, and do not come from beings with moral status. Quasi-testimony is offered as common ground for discussing instruments and testimony as sources of knowledge.
- Mitchell Green and Jan G. Michel 2022 What Might Machines Mean? — The essay asks whether artificial speakers can perform speech acts in the technical sense used in philosophy of language and answers yes, under specified conditions. It separates verbal signaling, an uncontroversial way in which machines communicate, from the performance of speech acts. It develops Austin's theory, Strawson's synthesis of Austin with Grice's speaker meaning, and a refinement that uses Armstrong's account of speaker meaning in terms of objectives rather than intentions, and extends the analysis to recorded, proxy and conditional speech acts. The proposal is that artificial speakers characteristically act as proxies performing speech acts on behalf of their human creators. The authors reply to objections, compare the view with alternatives such as quasi-assertion, which they say it sharpens without attributing intentions to machines, and end sceptical that the strategy covers every type of speech act.
- Fintan Mallory 2023 Fictionalism about Chatbots — Published in Ergo 10, article 38. The paper proposes a fictionalist treatment of chatbot output, on which users' engagement with a chatbot's apparent speech is understood through fiction rather than by taking the chatbot to perform genuine speech acts. (Description based on the title and on how later papers characterise the view; the published abstract could not be retrieved.)
- Reto Gubelmann 2024 Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now) – A Kantian-Cum-Pragmatist Case — Gubelmann asks whether current or foreseeable transformer-based LLMs could be language users in a way comparable to humans and answers no. Following Austin and Searle, he takes the speech act to be the basic unit of linguistic communication, and following Davidson and mainstream philosophy of action he holds that action requires intention; his argument is that to be a speaker a being must be able to illocute, that illocuting requires intentions, and that LLMs have none. His test for intention is whether one can sensibly distinguish a system's malfunctioning from its deliberately doing the wrong thing; for ChatGPT, for an imagined AI assistant that cleans up and translates a customer's order, and for Green and Michel's RoboCop, he argues no such distinction can be drawn. He grounds the lack of intention in Kant's distinction between mechanisms, whose purposes are imposed from outside, and organisms, which organise and maintain themselves and so have goals of their own; he separates material, cognitive and moral autonomy and argues that intentional action requires autonomous goal-setting, which LLMs lack because they do not strive to maintain themselves and their goals are externally fixed. He nonetheless argues that LLMs have cognitive autonomy, since they organise their own internal functional differentiation during training and adapt to new tasks, which makes them mechanisms with organismic traits that strain Kant's dichotomy. He concludes that LLMs are a first step toward non-biological agents that would no longer be artificial, that this development may be long, and, tentatively, that cognitive autonomy without material autonomy lends some support to dualism. A footnote leaves open that LLMs might understand language, since understanding lacks the tie to agency that speaking has.
- Patrick Butlin 2024 The agency in language agents — Language agents are AI systems that combine a large language model with other elements so as to interact with an environment without being reset; they range from basic LLM chatbots to systems with memory, reflection and structured planning. Goldstein and Kirk-Giannini argue that some have beliefs and desires, but Butlin first asks whether they are agents at all, given that they select outputs by sampling from a language model. He applies a criterion developed in earlier work: an entity is an agent if and only if it can produce outputs explained by its own sensitivity to instrumental value, meaning that it has systematically modified itself, through learning or reasoning, in response to information about what conduces to a goal over multi-step interaction; outputs owed solely to design or evolution do not count. On this criterion some language agents are agents and others are borderline. Basic chatbots built on pre-trained models with memory could qualify through in-context learning from feedback, but whether they do is an empirical matter. Chatbots built on models fine-tuned by reinforcement learning from human feedback are agents, with the caveats that rewards attach to single responses rather than whole conversations and that only limited fine-tuning is used. Park and colleagues' generative agents appear to be agents because they store observations and reflect on them, though they do little evaluation. Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that Skiba, fictionalism and the other named views share an "agent-first order of explanation". The thesis needs this for its target to be one unified position.

- Mallory's fictionalism, as far as I can tell from how it is characterised, concerns how users engage with chatbot output, namely through make-believe. I am not sure it says anything about whether a speech act requires an individuable performer. It may be neutral on record-change, or even compatible with it.
- Skiba's "norm-based argument" seems to say that LLMs cannot be subject to assertoric norms. That is a claim about norms, not obviously the thesis's claim that the speaker must be fixed before the act is. The abstract also says his view needs "pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction", which suggests he does not treat the record as secondary.
- Butlin and Viebahn make assertion a norm-governed social practice involving sanctioning. That is already close to the scorekeeping picture the thesis offers as an alternative.
- Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is explicitly a graded, emergence-based account, not a simple performer-first one.

So "no one performs, but the record changes" may be nearer to what some named targets allow than the thesis admits.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** Gubelmann explicitly holds that being a speaker requires illocuting, and that illocuting requires intention. Proxy accounts explicitly assign the act to a performer. Those two alone make the agent-first target real. My doubts about Skiba and Mallory rest on memory of abstracts, not on the texts, so I cannot say confidently that they reject the assumption. At most the thesis overgeneralises across the group.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis does not need each target to hold the assumption as an explicit doctrine. It needs the trichotomy to be exhaustive in the dispute as it is actually framed.** The claim is that the debate's options are "LLM performs", "proxy performs" and "no one performs", and that this menu leaves out the record-change-without-performer case. The objector concedes that Gubelmann (illocuting requires intention, and being a speaker requires illocuting) and the proxy accounts (the act is assigned to a performer) are agent-first. Those two already occupy two of the three cells, and the "no speech act" cell is Gubelmann's own verdict. So the menu is real. Whether Mallory or Skiba also share it affects how many authors the thesis can cite, not whether the exhaustiveness claim is false.

**2. The objector's counterexamples mostly confirm the target.**

- **Skiba's norm-based argument is agent-first.** "LLMs cannot be subject to assertoric norms, so they cannot assert" has a hidden premise: assertion requires a norm-bearer, someone the norms bind. That is the order of explanation the thesis targets, since it fixes who can be a subject of norms and only then says what was done. That the same paper invokes pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction shows he treats the record as a supplement. It does not show he treats it as primary. The thesis says this explicitly when it reclassifies pragmatics as the primary theory.
- **Mallory's fictionalism is agent-first via fiction.** The make-believe story is that the chatbot is a character who says things. The act is routed through a fictional performer, so "who is the speaker?" is still answered first, and the answer is a pretended agent. Fictionalism is therefore the proxy view with the proxy moved inside the pretence.
- **Butlin and Viebahn are allies, not counterexamples.** If their sanction-based practice account is close to scorekeeping, the thesis is extending a respectable resource. A rival who partly anticipated it does not refute it. And as I recall, they conclude that chatbot outputs can be assertions. That answers the performer question in the affirmative and stays on the menu.
- **Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is graded but still performer-indexed.** It says what the system does in a partial way. A graded performer is still a performer, and the account never considers a record change with no performer at all.

**3. The "partly verbal" claim is untouched.** It rests on the proxy view and the no-speech-act view differing only over who is assigned the commitment. That holds whatever the other authors say.

## VERDICT

**The defence holds against this objection.** The objector rates it 2/5 and concedes that the two positions the thesis most needs, Gubelmann and the proxy accounts, really are agent-first. Skiba and Mallory are defensible as agent-first on the arguments above, though I have not checked them against the texts.

The defence has two limits:

- **Attribution.** The claim that all four named views share one assumption is stronger than the thesis requires and not secured. The thesis should say the dispute's option space is agent-first, and that Gubelmann and the proxy views make it so explicitly. This corrects the target description. It does not narrow the thesis, whose claim is still that the trichotomy is non-exhaustive.
- **A different objection that would be serious.** Nothing here touches overgeneration. If speech acts are individuated by record effect with no performer, a thermometer reading or a forecast display also changes common ground, so what makes the LLM turn an assertion and not mere information? Scorekeeping, in Lewis and especially in Brandom, requires participants who undertake commitments. The thesis's "downstream commitment-assignment" move may therefore smuggle the performer back in. If the thesis fails, I expect it to fail there and not on misattribution.

response_text:
**ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that performing a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role, not by the speaker's intention or standing. If that is right, record effect is sufficient for the act.

But many things alter the conversational record, and none of them performs a speech act:
- A thermometer reading, a forecast display, a Ouija board pointer, a fortune-cookie slip and a wind-scattered page of text can each be taken up, challenged and cited.
- A mis-set road sign changes what is mutually taken for granted.
- On the thesis, each of these is an assertion made by no one. A chatbot apology would likewise be an apology made by no one. That is incoherent, since apologising is a way of owning a wrong (cf. Magnus et al.).

The thesis has two ways out, and both are costly:
1. Restrict the account to outputs in linguistic form that users treat as coming from an interlocutor. This reintroduces an agent-like role, whether a real or a presumed speaker, so the order of explanation reverts to agent-first.
2. Say commitments are assigned downstream to the deployer or the user. This collapses the view into the proxy account, and "partly verbal" becomes "wholly proxy".

Either the thesis overgenerates or it loses its novelty. The defender already flagged that scorekeeping (Lewis, Brandom) presupposes participants who undertake commitments.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** The overgeneration dilemma is the standard objection to record-first views and bites directly. Only a principled account of which record-changers count as acts, one that does not smuggle the performer back in, would answer it.

Reflexion, which evaluates its own performance and feeds the lessons into later action selection, is an unambiguous case. In several cases the answer depends on hard empirical questions about what functions an LLM has acquired in training. On desire, Butlin argues that the requirements are significantly more stringent than those for agency: language agents represent their goals, but he proposes two further necessary conditions, that the state be used in practical reasoning answerable to standards of conduciveness to the objective, and that it be acquired and modified through learning and reasoning that tend to produce a coherent, integrated set. Generative agents, whose goals are fixed by their designers, do not meet the second, and it is uncertain whether they meet the first. He concludes that many language agents are genuine agents, that it is doubtful whether existing ones have desires, and that the conditions he proposes are nonetheless compatible with desire in AI.
- Chirag Arora 2024 Proxy Assertions and Agency: The Case of Machine-Assertions — Speech-enabled devices increasingly serve as sources of information. Some philosophers argue that machine utterances should be conceptualised as assertions because they resemble human speech phenomenologically and serve the same communicative functions. Arora rejects this, identifying theoretical and practical difficulties with treating machine utterances as assertions on functionalist grounds, and argues that they are better understood as proxy assertions made by or on behalf of the designers and deployers of the machines. Existing accounts of proxy assertion need refinement, which the paper supplies, and the refined view has implications for the design of such devices, particularly those using machine learning.
- Iwan Williams and Tim Bayne 2024 Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion — The paper examines the Thesis of Chatbot Assertion, the claim that LLM-powered chatbots can assert and that some of their current outputs are assertions. The authors give reasons in favour of the thesis and argue it deserves to be taken seriously, while holding that recent objections to it are substantial. They consider two proposed ways of resolving the tension, proxy-assertion and fictionalism, and find both inadequate. Drawing on how assertion emerges, they introduce a new category, proto-assertion, and argue that treating chatbots as proto-assertors resolves the dilemma.
- Nuhu Osman Attah 2025 Do language models lack communicative intentions? — Attah examines the communicative intention argument advanced by Bender and Koller, Bender and colleagues, Shanahan and Montemayor: genuine linguistic competence requires communicative intention, language models have no mechanism for entertaining such intentions, so they are only stochastic parrots. Using Mahowald and colleagues' distinction between formal and functional linguistic competence, he locates the dispute in functional competence. Against the first premise read in a strong Gricean way, which requires high-order representation of other minds, he argues that it is empirically untenable, citing young children, non-human animals and work on early hominin communication, so the argument must fall back on a basic intention to produce an illocutionary or perlocutionary effect in a hearer. He then sets three desiderata for a definition of intention (functional rather than phenomenological, consistent with the causal theory of action and representationalism, and not presupposing full agency) and proposes a control conception: intentions are internal states that control a system's dynamics so as to bring about an action in a situation that calls for one, where control means solving Wu's Many-Many Problem through attention-like selection. Taking Levelt's Blueprint of the Speaker (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) as the functional template, he argues that classical dialogue systems built on partially observable Markov decision processes fit it, with belief-state tracking estimating the user's intention, and that transformer models plausibly recapitulate the same pipeline. To the objection that the extra-linguistic purpose behind speech is missing, he replies that the design context supplies language models with purposes, thinner than human ones and mediated by human designers. Intention on this account is graded: a coffee machine has almost none, ELIZA a little, and how much ChatGPT has is still open. He concludes that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from language models, and states that he takes the real difference to be the absence of mental and metalinguistic agency.
- Xabier E. Barandiaran and Lola S. Almendros 2025 Transforming agency: On the mode of existence of large language models — The paper asks how LLMs such as ChatGPT should be characterised ontologically, between inflationary and deflationary accounts, with a focus on their status as agents. After explaining their architecture, processing, training and the extensions that turn them into agent-like systems, it argues that LLMs fail necessary conditions for autonomous agency on embodied theories of mind: individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry. It characterises them instead as an interlocutor or linguistic automaton, a library-that-talks, able to perform tasks that are not purposeful but are purpose-structured and purpose-bounded. Interaction with them can still be experienced as genuine conversation, and the coupling of humans with LLMs produces 'midtended' forms of agency that differ from earlier technological extensions of human agency.
- Anna Puzio 2025 The Material Agency of a Large Language Model — Puzio observes that agency is highly contested in the ethics of LLMs and that the debate relies on traditional, property-based, individualistic and anthropocentric conceptions of it. Drawing on Actor-Network Theory and New Materialism, she proposes a relational, network-based view that admits non-human agency and several forms of agency. She argues that the materiality of LLMs has been overlooked, including their conditions of production, their realisation in devices and their effects on human bodies, and that attending to it shows how LLMs are bound up with culture, material practices and social values. The focus then shifts from the individual user as sole agent to networks of actors, including workers, companies, environmental factors and technologies, which changes the ethical questions that should be asked about LLMs.
- Patrick Butlin and Emanuel Viebahn 2025 AI Assertion — The fluency of generative AI has prompted debate about whether these systems understand language; less discussed is whether they can perform speech acts, in particular assertion. The authors hold that to assert, an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and must be capable of being sanctioned by the agents it interacts with, the second condition reflecting the fact that assertion is a norm-governed social practice. Pre-trained language models that have not been fine-tuned fail the first condition. Models fine-tuned for groundedness or correctness may meet the first condition but fail the second. AI systems can nonetheless be used to produce proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.
- P. D. Magnus, Alessandra Buccella and Jason D'Cruz 2025 Chatbot apologies: Beyond bullshit — Apologies do important work for moral agents: expressing remorse, taking responsibility and repairing trust. LLM-based chatbots produce outputs with the linguistic form of an apology, generated by pattern matching. The authors argue that chatbots lack the linguistic and moral agency needed to apologise, and develop the claim that chatbot apologies are bullshit by examining what a morally serious apology involves, what agency is required to perform one linguistically, and what agency is required for it to matter morally. They draw out implications for chatbot design and for how people should understand these systems.
- Lukas Skiba 2026 Artificial Speech Acts — The article asks whether large language models can perform speech acts. It presents a norm-based argument against LLM assertion and extends it to reach a negative conclusion about LLM speech acts generally. The resulting no-speech-act view is related to other ways of conceptualising LLM output: it conflicts with the common view that LLMs bullshit, and it helps to tell apart two competing externalist theories of reference for artificially generated expressions. A challenge to the view is discussed together with a strategy for answering it. The author suggests that understanding LLM output requires combining existing meta-semantic theories with pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction.

response_text:
**ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that uptake-dependence makes "merely interpreted" ill-formed for acts like advising, promising and apologising. The term "uptake-constitution" carries two readings, and the thesis needs both.

- **Reading A (Austin, Hornsby, Langton).** Uptake is a necessary condition on the success of an act that a speaker attempted. Without the hearer's recognition, the attempt misfires or is silenced. This is plausible and well supported in the tradition.
- **Reading B (the thesis's novelty).** A hearer's interpretation of text as advice, with no speaker attempt behind it, can help bring about the act, with the "speaker slot" filled by a network. This is the interesting claim, since it is what makes the denial baseline ill-formed and reverses the classification of fictionalism.

On Reading A, uptake presupposes an attempt to take up. A chatbot with no attempt then yields no act, and "merely interpreted" is still the correct verdict. Fictionalism then classifies exactly as the denials do, and the "opposite classification" claim collapses. The cited tradition supports only Reading A. Reading B needs the further premise that uptake can supply or replace the speaker-side condition, and that premise is not supplied. Relabelling the network as the speaker either reintroduces production-side conditions or is stipulation.

The argument runs on A for plausibility and B for payoff, so it cannot be run on either alone.

STRENGTH: 3/5. This is a genuine problem, but the thesis could answer it by defending B directly, for example through Puzio-style relational agency or hearer-constituted social acts such as naming or conferring status.
