Candidate:
{
  "thesis": "The dispute assumes that a speech act occurs only if some agent performs it, so that the options are 'LLM performs', 'human proxy performs' or 'no one performs'. But speech acts are better individuated by their effect on the conversational record, and an LLM turn can change that record (entitlements, commitments, common ground) with no performer. 'No speech act' and 'speech act by someone' are therefore not exhaustive.",
  "move_type": "reframing",
  "sketch": "Denials, proxy accounts, fictionalism and proto-assertion all share an agent-first order of explanation: first fix who the speaker is, then say what was done. Lewisian scorekeeping and Austinian uptake suggest the reverse: an utterance is an assertion if the record is updated by it as a proposal that p is common ground subject to challenge. An LLM turn that users take up, challenge and cite does alter the record. The relevant question, who is answerable for p now, is then a downstream question about commitment-assignment, not about whether an act happened. The proxy view and the no-speech-act view differ only over who gets assigned the commitment, which makes the disagreement partly verbal. The premise it turns on is that performance of a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role and not by the speaker's intention or standing. The thesis reclassifies Skiba's 'pragmatic theories of human\u2013LLM interaction' as the primary theory rather than a supplement to metasemantics. It also separates the question 'was something asserted?' from 'who asserted?', which the literature runs together.",
  "target": "The shared agent-first assumption of Skiba, Gubelmann, proxy accounts and fictionalism."
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that Skiba, fictionalism and the other named views share an "agent-first order of explanation". The thesis needs this for its target to be one unified position.

- Mallory's fictionalism, as far as I can tell from how it is characterised, concerns how users engage with chatbot output, namely through make-believe. I am not sure it says anything about whether a speech act requires an individuable performer. It may be neutral on record-change, or even compatible with it.
- Skiba's "norm-based argument" seems to say that LLMs cannot be subject to assertoric norms. That is a claim about norms, not obviously the thesis's claim that the speaker must be fixed before the act is. The abstract also says his view needs "pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction", which suggests he does not treat the record as secondary.
- Butlin and Viebahn make assertion a norm-governed social practice involving sanctioning. That is already close to the scorekeeping picture the thesis offers as an alternative.
- Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is explicitly a graded, emergence-based account, not a simple performer-first one.

So "no one performs, but the record changes" may be nearer to what some named targets allow than the thesis admits.

**STRENGTH: 2/5.** Gubelmann explicitly holds that being a speaker requires illocuting, and that illocuting requires intention. Proxy accounts explicitly assign the act to a performer. Those two alone make the agent-first target real. My doubts about Skiba and Mallory rest on memory of abstracts, not on the texts, so I cannot say confidently that they reject the assumption. At most the thesis overgeneralises across the group.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis does not need each target to hold the assumption as an explicit doctrine. It needs the trichotomy to be exhaustive in the dispute as it is actually framed.** The claim is that the debate's options are "LLM performs", "proxy performs" and "no one performs", and that this menu leaves out the record-change-without-performer case. The objector concedes that Gubelmann (illocuting requires intention, and being a speaker requires illocuting) and the proxy accounts (the act is assigned to a performer) are agent-first. Those two already occupy two of the three cells, and the "no speech act" cell is Gubelmann's own verdict. So the menu is real. Whether Mallory or Skiba also share it affects how many authors the thesis can cite, not whether the exhaustiveness claim is false.

**2. The objector's counterexamples mostly confirm the target.**

- **Skiba's norm-based argument is agent-first.** "LLMs cannot be subject to assertoric norms, so they cannot assert" has a hidden premise: assertion requires a norm-bearer, someone the norms bind. That is the order of explanation the thesis targets, since it fixes who can be a subject of norms and only then says what was done. That the same paper invokes pragmatic theories of human–LLM interaction shows he treats the record as a supplement. It does not show he treats it as primary. The thesis says this explicitly when it reclassifies pragmatics as the primary theory.
- **Mallory's fictionalism is agent-first via fiction.** The make-believe story is that the chatbot is a character who says things. The act is routed through a fictional performer, so "who is the speaker?" is still answered first, and the answer is a pretended agent. Fictionalism is therefore the proxy view with the proxy moved inside the pretence.
- **Butlin and Viebahn are allies, not counterexamples.** If their sanction-based practice account is close to scorekeeping, the thesis is extending a respectable resource. A rival who partly anticipated it does not refute it. And as I recall, they conclude that chatbot outputs can be assertions. That answers the performer question in the affirmative and stays on the menu.
- **Williams and Bayne's proto-assertion is graded but still performer-indexed.** It says what the system does in a partial way. A graded performer is still a performer, and the account never considers a record change with no performer at all.

**3. The "partly verbal" claim is untouched.** It rests on the proxy view and the no-speech-act view differing only over who is assigned the commitment. That holds whatever the other authors say.

## VERDICT

**The defence holds against this objection.** The objector rates it 2/5 and concedes that the two positions the thesis most needs, Gubelmann and the proxy accounts, really are agent-first. Skiba and Mallory are defensible as agent-first on the arguments above, though I have not checked them against the texts.

The defence has two limits:

- **Attribution.** The claim that all four named views share one assumption is stronger than the thesis requires and not secured. The thesis should say the dispute's option space is agent-first, and that Gubelmann and the proxy views make it so explicitly. This corrects the target description. It does not narrow the thesis, whose claim is still that the trichotomy is non-exhaustive.
- **A different objection that would be serious.** Nothing here touches overgeneration. If speech acts are individuated by record effect with no performer, a thermometer reading or a forecast display also changes common ground, so what makes the LLM turn an assertion and not mere information? Scorekeeping, in Lewis and especially in Brandom, requires participants who undertake commitments. The thesis's "downstream commitment-assignment" move may therefore smuggle the performer back in. If the thesis fails, I expect it to fail there and not on misattribution.

[KILLER (PROVES TOO MUCH)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that performing a speech act is constituted by its record-changing role, not by the speaker's intention or standing. If that is right, record effect is sufficient for the act.

But many things alter the conversational record, and none of them performs a speech act:
- A thermometer reading, a forecast display, a Ouija board pointer, a fortune-cookie slip and a wind-scattered page of text can each be taken up, challenged and cited.
- A mis-set road sign changes what is mutually taken for granted.
- On the thesis, each of these is an assertion made by no one. A chatbot apology would likewise be an apology made by no one. That is incoherent, since apologising is a way of owning a wrong (cf. Magnus et al.).

The thesis has two ways out, and both are costly:
1. Restrict the account to outputs in linguistic form that users treat as coming from an interlocutor. This reintroduces an agent-like role, whether a real or a presumed speaker, so the order of explanation reverts to agent-first.
2. Say commitments are assigned downstream to the deployer or the user. This collapses the view into the proxy account, and "partly verbal" becomes "wholly proxy".

Either the thesis overgenerates or it loses its novelty. The defender already flagged that scorekeeping (Lewis, Brandom) presupposes participants who undertake commitments.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** The overgeneration dilemma is the standard objection to record-first views and bites directly. Only a principled account of which record-changers count as acts, one that does not smuggle the performer back in, would answer it.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The dilemma assumes record effect has to be *any* record effect. The thesis needs only one route to the record: being put forward as a move in a practice with deontic structure.**

A thermometer reading changes the record as evidence. Users infer from a causal source to a fact, and the reading carries no proposal that p be common ground. It cannot be asked "how do you know?" or be held to a retraction. A wind-scattered page and a mis-set road sign are likewise taken up as symptoms or malfunctions, not as moves. An LLM turn works differently. Its conventional linguistic meaning is offered as a candidate for common ground. It sits in a turn-taking structure, it is open to challenge and to demands for justification, and it responds to those demands. That is Stalnaker's essential effect plus Lewisian accommodation and Austinian uptake, and none of it is available to a fortune-cookie slip. So the criterion is a *role in the scoreboard*, not a mere causal effect. This is a principled line, and it is the one the literature already draws between evidence and testimony.

**2. The role is not a performer smuggled back in.** Brandom, whom the objector's own point relies on, makes discursive agency *status-conferred*. To be a participant who undertakes commitments is to be treated as one by scorekeepers. This is the thesis's reversal of explanatory order. Scorekeepers (the users) are required, but the LLM need not be an agent antecedently. A slot in the scoreboard, "source of p", is filled by the practice of taking the turn as a move, in the way Foucault's author-function is filled without anyone fixing the author's mental life first. Role-first is not agent-first.

**3. Horn 2 does not collapse into the proxy view.** The proxy view says the deployer or user *performs* the act of asserting p. The thesis says the deployer may be *answerable* for p, as a publisher or editor is answerable for a printed claim, without having asserted it. Answerability for a record item is not performance of the act that produced it. There are also cases where no one is answerable. Anonymous rumour, an unattributable inscription and a corrupted wire-service item all update the record and invite challenge while the commitment-slot stays empty or contested. That is what separates "was something asserted?" from "who asserted?".

**4. On apology.** The apology case shows that expressives are not individuated by record effect. They require the owning of a wrong. But the dispute in the literature is about assertion and the assertive family, which is exactly what scorekeeping individuates. So the thesis need not claim that every speech act type is record-constituted. This is a difference between act types, and the thesis never claimed uniformity.

## VERDICT

**The defence does not hold. The thesis fails at the premise that performing a speech act is *constituted* by record-changing role.**

- **The criterion in point 1 restores a performer by another name.** What separates the LLM turn from the thermometer is that it is treated as a move by a responsive participant with a source that can be challenged. If that status suffices, then on Brandom's and Dennett's interpretivism the LLM *is* the performer, by status. That is the "LLM performs" cell with a deflationary account of performing, not a fourth cell. If the status does not suffice, the line between thermometer and LLM has no principled basis.
- **The "no performer" reading has a cost the defence never repaid.** The thesis's own record items are entitlements and commitments. Those are deontic statuses *of someone*. A commitment with an empty bearer cannot be violated, sanctioned or discharged. Only common ground survives bearerless, and a *proposal* to add to it is still a putting-forward. "Put forward by no one" is not a coherent act description. It is a record effect.
- **What survives is not the thesis.** What is left is the claim that LLM turns have record effects and that who is answerable is a separate question. Gubelmann-style deniers already accept both. They say the effect is informational and not an act. So the distinction does not show that "no speech act" and "speech act by someone" are non-exhaustive. It restates the first option with a record effect added.
- **The apology case reinforces this.** Restricting the account to assertives, or adding a status criterion, would be the accumulation of qualifications that kills a thesis. I will not make those moves to rescue it.

The thesis is dead as stated. The separation of "was something asserted?" from "who is answerable?" is worth keeping as a distinction, but it does not defeat the trichotomy.

Candidate:
{
  "thesis": "The debate is about production-constitution (a speech act exists in virtue of facts about the speaker), whereas the relational picture suggests uptake-constitution (illocutionary force is fixed in the hearer's securing of uptake). These two give opposite classifications of fictionalism and of the 'text that humans interpret as speech acts' deflationary option.",
  "move_type": "reframing",
  "sketch": "Every denial and attributing view asks whether the machine has the intentions, norms or agency to produce the act. The fallback 'it only produces text that humans interpret as such' treats interpretation as epistemically downstream of a fact about production. Puzio's relational view and the Austin-Hornsby-Langton tradition on uptake suggest another structure. Some illocutions, such as promising, advising, apologising and warning, are completed or constituted in an interaction in which a hearer takes them up and so incurs entitlements. On a strict uptake-constitutive reading, a human interpreting a chatbot's text as advice does not merely misdescribe a non-act. It may help bring about an act of advice whose speaker slot is filled by the network, with the 'interpretation' being part of the act. This makes the standard denial 'merely interpreted' ill-formed for uptake-dependent acts, while leaving it fine for acts like assertion that may be production-constituted. Fictionalism then becomes the view that users deliberately withhold uptake. The key premise is that the speech acts differ in whether their constitutive conditions are speaker-side or hearer-side, so that no uniform answer across assertion, promise and apology is available.",
  "target": "The 'merely interpreted' deflationary baseline shared by the denials, and Mallory's and Williams and Bayne's treatment of interpretation as downstream of production."
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] ATTEMPT. The weak point is the premise that the denial literature, including Mallory and Williams and Bayne, treats interpretation as epistemically downstream of production facts. That is the shared "merely interpreted" baseline the thesis attacks.

- **Mallory.** On the summary here, fictionalism is a claim about the hearer's stance: users engage with chatbot output through make-believe. That is already a hearer-side account of what is going on, so it is hard to call it a production-constitutive view. The thesis then recasts fictionalism as "withholding uptake", which suggests it is closer to Mallory than to a target.
- **Williams and Bayne.** They reject fictionalism and proxy-assertion and defend proto-assertion, in terms of chatbot functions and how assertion emerges. I don't recall them endorsing "merely interpreted" as a baseline. They treat it as one of the dilemma's horns.
- **Butlin and Viebahn.** Their second condition, that the entity be capable of being sanctioned by interlocutors, is explicitly social and interactional. It is not a purely speaker-internal intention requirement, so "every denial asks about the machine's intentions, norms or agency" is too uniform.
- **Green and Michel.** They build on Austin and Strawson, so uptake is arguably already in their framework.

So the thesis may be aimed at a composite strawman. I can't verify the exact wording of these papers from memory.

STRENGTH: 2/5. The attack lands only partly. Most of the authors do locate speech-act status in facts about the system, even where those facts are relational, and the thesis can reasonably retreat to targeting that structure rather than the particular authors. I'm unsure about the details of Mallory's and Williams and Bayne's views, so I won't rate it higher.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

The objection runs together two things the thesis keeps apart: hearer-side facts and uptake-constitution. The thesis does not say the denial literature ignores hearers. It says the literature treats facts about hearers as explanatory or evidential and never as constitutive of the illocution. Each of the four cases fits that pattern.

**Mallory.** Fictionalism is hearer-oriented, but it is a hypothesis about why users behave as they do, given that no speech act has occurred. The make-believe stance explains the appearance of assertion while the assertion itself is absent. The hearer's stance does no constitutive work. So fictionalism is a hearer-side psychology bolted onto a production-side verdict (no speaker, no act). The thesis does not treat fictionalism as a target but reclassifies it as one view among others: on an uptake view it becomes the position that users withhold the very thing that would complete the act. Mallory's two-part structure, a verdict about production plus a story about users, is what the thesis diagnoses. That the thesis and Mallory agree that the fictionalist user performs no act is expected, since both classify that case the same way. The classifications come apart for the user who takes the output at face value, and that is the case the "merely interpreted" baseline exists to handle.

**Williams and Bayne.** The objector says the "text that humans interpret as speech acts" option is a horn of their dilemma, not their baseline. That helps the thesis. The thesis targets the deflationary option as a live fallback in the debate, and the objector confirms it is one. What matters is that interpretation is placed downstream of a fact about production, which is how the horn is structured. Proto-assertion is also defined by the chatbot's functions and their emergence, which is a speaker-side specification.

**Butlin and Viebahn.** Their sanctionability condition is social in content but it is a capacity condition on the candidate speaker: whether the entity can be sanctioned. It is not a condition that some particular hearer actually took the act up and incurred entitlements. A relational property of the producer is still a production-side constituent. Uptake-constitution requires the hearer's actual securing of uptake to be part of what makes the act the act, which differs from the speaker having a capacity that hearers could exercise.

**Green and Michel.** Building on Austin and Strawson does not commit one to uptake-constitution. Austin's felicity conditions are largely speaker-side (appropriate persons, procedures, intentions), with uptake as a contested extra. Hornsby and Langton had to argue against the mainstream reading to get uptake into the constitution of some illocutions. That the Austinian lineage is invoked therefore shows the structure is available, not that the denial literature uses it.

So the target is a structure, the direction of constitution, and author-by-author attribution is not needed to establish it.

## VERDICT

The defence holds against this objection, and it does so without narrowing the thesis. The distinction between hearer-side explanation and hearer-side constitution is already in the thesis and does the work. The objector's examples, sanctionability and make-believe, are all hearer-involving without being uptake-constitutive, which is the point at issue.

Two costs remain. First, the word "every" in the sketch is too strong for Butlin and Viebahn as stated, and "the shared question the literature asks" should be argued rather than asserted. This is a correction of wording and does not shrink the claim. Second, the objector is right that I cannot verify the papers from memory, and neither can they. The misattribution charge is therefore unproven, though the defence does not depend on the exact wording.

The objection is weak (2/5, as it rates itself). The thesis's real exposure lies elsewhere: whether an uptake-constituted illocution can have a "speaker slot filled by the network" when Austinian and Hornsby-style uptake presupposes a speaker with some standing, and whether that move quietly reintroduces the production-side conditions the reframing was meant to bypass. A different objection should test that.

[KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that uptake-dependence makes "merely interpreted" ill-formed for acts like advising, promising and apologising. The term "uptake-constitution" carries two readings, and the thesis needs both.

- **Reading A (Austin, Hornsby, Langton).** Uptake is a necessary condition on the success of an act that a speaker attempted. Without the hearer's recognition, the attempt misfires or is silenced. This is plausible and well supported in the tradition.
- **Reading B (the thesis's novelty).** A hearer's interpretation of text as advice, with no speaker attempt behind it, can help bring about the act, with the "speaker slot" filled by a network. This is the interesting claim, since it is what makes the denial baseline ill-formed and reverses the classification of fictionalism.

On Reading A, uptake presupposes an attempt to take up. A chatbot with no attempt then yields no act, and "merely interpreted" is still the correct verdict. Fictionalism then classifies exactly as the denials do, and the "opposite classification" claim collapses. The cited tradition supports only Reading A. Reading B needs the further premise that uptake can supply or replace the speaker-side condition, and that premise is not supplied. Relabelling the network as the speaker either reintroduces production-side conditions or is stipulation.

The argument runs on A for plausibility and B for payoff, so it cannot be run on either alone.

STRENGTH: 3/5. This is a genuine problem, but the thesis could answer it by defending B directly, for example through Puzio-style relational agency or hearer-constituted social acts such as naming or conferring status.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

The equivocation charge assumes the thesis borrows plausibility from Reading A and cashes it out as Reading B. But the sketch does not run the two together. It says "on a *strict* uptake-constitutive reading" and "may help bring about", and its key premise is that the constitutive conditions of different acts sit on different sides. The thesis is explicitly Reading B. The question is whether B is independently supported, and there are three resources.

1. **Austin's conventionalism.** Austin and Strawson treat illocutions as conventional acts, performed by invoking a procedure under suitable circumstances. Strawson's point in "Intention and Convention in Speech Acts" is that a conventional act does not require a Gricean intention to perform that act. So the objector's premise that uptake presupposes a specific attempt is not a datum of the tradition. It is one reading of it, the Gricean one, and the thesis targets production-constitution precisely because the denials import that reading.

2. **Speech acts without the corresponding attempt.** Several lines of work already detach illocutionary status from the speaker's intending it:
   - Austin's insincere promises.
   - Accidental insults and warnings.
   - Maitra's and McGowan's work on subordinating speech and covert exercitives, where what the speech enacts is fixed by context and uptake-like social uptake, not by what the speaker meant.
   
   So Reading B is a limiting case of an existing trend, not a novelty.

3. **Conferralism.** Searle's status functions and Ásta's conferralism hold that social properties are constituted by others' responses. Money has no intentions. If "advisor" and "warner" are conferred statuses, then a hearer's uptake can fill a role without a prior attempt. This also answers "stipulation". The speaker slot is filled the way any conferred status is, by recognition within a practice.

A warning sign makes the case concrete. It warns every passer-by, yet at the moment of reading no one is attempting anything. If that is not a defeater for "uptake presupposes a current attempt", the objector owes an account of why it fails here.

Finally, on Reading A the thesis would lose its "opposite classification" claim, which is why it was never offered as A. The charge shows that B carries the whole weight, and the thesis accepts that.

## VERDICT

The defence beats the charge of equivocation but does not rescue the thesis. The inconsistency charge fails, since the thesis is B and says so. The 3/5 stands, though, as a charge that B is unsupported for the acts the thesis names.

- **The cited tradition supports only A.** Austin–Hornsby–Langton as cited in the sketch gives A. B rests on a different literature (conferralism, Maitra, McGowan) that the sketch does not use.

- **The B resources fit the wrong acts.** Status declaratives and norm-enacting speech are cases where the act's content is a status or permissibility fact, and recognition really can constitute those. Promising and apologising are different. A promise needs a bearer of the obligation, and an apology needs someone who takes responsibility. Hearer uptake can create the hearer's entitlements, but it cannot create an obligor who can be bound. If the network cannot bear commitments, "the speaker slot filled by the network" is stipulation. The thesis's own examples, promising and apologising, are the ones where B is weakest.

- **The warning-sign case cuts against the thesis.** The sign warns because someone put it there, with intent. The analogue is the developer or deployer, which relocates the speaker to a production-side fact. The reframing was meant to bypass exactly that.

- **Conferralism changes the dispute.** If "advice" is a conferred status, the denier can grant every social fact (users treat it as advice, incur entitlements, act on it) and still say no speech act in the production sense occurred. The "opposite classification" then reflects a choice of what "speech act" names, not a substantive disagreement.

What survives is a diagnosis: the denials treat interpretation as downstream of production, and that is a substantive, non-neutral commitment for acts with hearer-side conditions. It is a good point, but it is not the thesis. Saving the positive claim would mean limiting it to warning and advice, and relocating the speaker to the deployer. That is hedging by accumulation, so I report the positive thesis as dead in its stated form.

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try
  this first.

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather
  than shrinking it into safety.

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.

Candidate:
{
  "thesis": "The assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output, which underlies both Gubelmann's malfunction-versus-deliberate test and Attah's Levelt-style planning template, is false even of human speakers. Much human illocution is incremental, with the force of the act settled by retrospective ownership, so the human-versus-LLM difference cannot be located in the presence of an intention.",
  "move_type": "counterexample",
  "sketch": "Both denials and attributions treat the speaker as having something like a conceptualised message and a communicative intention that the Formulator then realises (Attah) or whose failure can be told apart from malfunction (Gubelmann). Barandiaran and Almendros likewise contrast the LLM's purpose-structured but not purposeful operation with human purposefulness. Counterexample: ordinary improvised talk. Speakers begin sentences without having settled what they will assert, discover the force of the utterance from where it goes ('I was going to say it was a warning, but I suppose it was an accusation'), and become committed by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn. Splitting such acts from their reflective ownership makes the intention post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal. Speech acts are therefore constituted by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting. This reframes the dispute: the question is whether LLM threads show the right pattern of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. This is an empirical question about interaction structure, not an issue about internal mental states. The premise it turns on is that retrospective force-fixing is not a marginal case.",
  "target": "Gubelmann's malfunction test, Attah's pipeline template for communicative intention, and the implicit human paradigm in Barandiaran and Almendros."
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that Gubelmann, Attah and Barandiaran and Almendros share the assumption that a speech-act intention exists prior to or alongside output. As I remember them, none of them is committed to that, so the attack on that assumption is partly aimed at nobody.

- **Attah:** He does not defend a prior-message view. He defines intention functionally, as a state that controls the system's dynamics to produce an action, and treats it as graded. He argues against the strong Gricean reading. His closing claim is that communicative intention is not the right ground for distinguishing humans from LLMs, locating the difference in mental and metalinguistic agency. That is close to the thesis's own conclusion, so the thesis attacks a view he has already given up. Levelt's Blueprint is also a template he borrows, not a thesis about timing.
- **Gubelmann:** His test asks whether we can sensibly distinguish malfunction from deliberately doing the wrong thing. This is a practice-level, diachronic criterion about how conduct is assessed, not a claim about a pre-formed message. His grounding is Kantian autonomy and self-maintenance, not planning. Davidsonian intention in acting does not require prior intention.
- **Barandiaran and Almendros:** Their conditions are individuality, normativity and interactional asymmetry, drawn from enactivism. These are not a prior-intention model, so naming them is a stretch.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** I am relying on memory of these papers. Gubelmann may still treat intention as a state of the agent, and Attah's Levelt template does posit a Conceptualizer stage. So the thesis can narrow its target, but as written it overstates what its named targets hold.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis says the assumption "underlies" the positions, not that their authors profess it.** A misattribution objection has to show that the positions can be stated without the assumption. It cannot rest on the authors' avowals.

- **Attah.** Even granting his functional, graded definition of intention, the definition is a *controlling state that produces the action*. That is causal and temporally prior to or concurrent with the output, which is exactly what the thesis denies. The Levelt template is not a neutral borrowing. Its Conceptualizer stage generates a preverbal message with its illocutionary purpose before the Formulator runs, so the pipeline fixes force upstream of articulation. Attah's final retreat to metalinguistic agency does not remove this. He needs the template to say what LLMs lack or have, and the template carries the prior-intention structure.
- **Gubelmann.** The malfunction-versus-deliberate test is only intelligible if there is a fact about what the agent meant to do, against which a deviation could count as an error and not as the act. "Deliberately doing the wrong thing" presupposes a deliberation or intending that the act expresses. Davidson's intention in acting is the "alongside" case. The thesis's counterexample goes further: in incremental talk, even concurrent force-settlement is missing.
- **Barandiaran and Almendros.** "Purposefulness" as the human contrast term trades on an agent-level purpose that the system's structure either realises or merely mimics. That is the implicit paradigm, and the thesis names it as implicit.

**2. The central claim is independent of the attribution.** Even if no named author held the assumption, the thesis's claim stands: much human illocution has its force settled retrospectively. That claim bears on any human-versus-LLM contrast that appeals to an intention present at the time of output, whoever states it.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold for the thesis as written.

**Attah.** His conclusion is that communicative intention is not the right ground for the human-LLM distinction. That is the thesis's own conclusion, so the thesis cannot present itself as refuting the shared assumption. The Conceptualizer point is real but narrow. It shows the template is prior-intention shaped, but he explicitly demotes the template's role.

**Gubelmann.** My "presupposes a fact about what the agent meant" argument is the weakest step. A practice-level, diachronic test of how conduct is assessed is exactly what the thesis recommends as the replacement. Reading a prior-intention commitment into it is a stretch, and if the reading fails, the thesis ends up endorsing his criterion while claiming to refute it.

**Barandiaran and Almendros.** The enactivist conditions of individuality, normativity and asymmetry are not a planning model. Calling this a "implicit human paradigm" is an unsupported inference.

Defence point 2 is the strongest, but it only shows the central claim could survive. It does not show the thesis survives. To rescue it I would have to drop two of the three targets, rewrite the claim as "a Levelt-style template misdescribes human illocution", and present the diachronic reframing as an extension of Gubelmann and Attah instead of a refutation. That is narrowing the thesis until the objection no longer touches it, which is hedging. The thesis as submitted, a counterexample to an assumption shared by all three, is dead on its attribution.

One further weakness the defence cannot fix: the example "I was going to say it was a warning, but..." itself reports a prior intention to say something warning-like. The thesis also rests on the unargued premise that retrospective force-fixing is not marginal.

[KILLER (COUNTEREXAMPLE)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that illocutionary force is *constituted* by a diachronic pattern of owning and retracting, so that the human-versus-LLM question becomes whether LLM threads show that pattern.

**Counterexample 1: the terminal utterance.** A hiker shouts "The ice is thin!" and is swept away. A dying declaration, a message in a bottle, or a last email sent before a fatal crash works the same way. There is no next turn, no taking up, no owning or disowning. Yet each is plainly a warning or an assertion. The thesis's constitutive claim gets these cases wrong. Retreating to counterfactual dispositions to own the act concedes that an internal state of the speaker fixes force, which is the thing the thesis set out to dismiss.

**Counterexample 2: the scripted retractor.** Take a bot with a rule: "if challenged, say 'I stand by that'; if corrected twice, say 'I retract that.'" It shows the pattern of owning and retracting while having no intention, so on the thesis's criterion it performs speech acts. Gubelmann's test and Attah's control conception would rightly separate it from a genuine speaker.

The thesis's own example also reports an *initial* intention to warn, so it shows revisable intention, not absent intention.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The thesis can answer by weakening "constituted" to "partly fixed" and by adding a requirement that the ownership be non-scripted. But that second addition reintroduces a state-based condition, and then the thesis no longer reframes the dispute.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The terminal utterance assumes the pattern must be the speaker's own later conduct.** The thesis's phrase "retrospective ownership" can be read at the level of the practice, as in Brandomian score-keeping. On that reading, commitments are attributed and enforced by an audience under norms. They do not require the speaker to endorse anything.

- The hiker's shout is a warning because it sits in a practice where such shouts are held to account. Had he shouted it knowing the ice was sound, he would have been blamed for deceiving. Wills, dying declarations and messages in bottles are owned by attribution to their author, often after the author is gone.
- No internal state of the speaker is smuggled back in. What fixes force is the normative status the community assigns, which is a diachronic pattern of taking up and holding to account.
- The thesis says "much" human illocution is incremental, not all. The terminal cases are the ones where force happens to be fixed at once or by third parties. They do not show that the pre-intention model is right for improvised talk.

**2. The scripted retractor is a degenerate sample of the pattern.** The thesis asks whether threads show "the right pattern" of taking up, owning and being held to earlier outputs. That pattern is rich:

- retracting when the output is shown inconsistent with other commitments;
- revising downstream claims after a retraction;
- recognising what an earlier statement commits one to.

A two-rule bot fails this by ordinary behavioural test, as ELIZA fails any extended probe. The criterion is robust across extended interaction. A bot that passed it would not be a mere script, and the intuition that it lacks intention would then be doing no work beyond the very prior-state assumption under dispute. The objection also cuts both ways. Gubelmann's malfunction test is itself a behavioural-pattern test applied to conduct, and the scripted bot would pass or fail it on the same grounds.

**3. The example reports revisable intention, not an intention that fixes force.** "I was going to say a warning" reports a provisional aim. The thesis's point is that the aim did not determine the act's force, since the force became an accusation. A defeasible aim that the act can overrule is not the intention the pipeline model needs.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold. Each reply works only by giving up something the thesis needs.

**Terminal utterances.** Moving constitution from the speaker's own retrospective ownership to the audience's score-keeping abandons the thesis's actual mechanism, which is that the speaker becomes committed "by endorsing or disowning it in the next turn." Audience attribution also over-generates for the LLM question. Users already attribute assertions, warnings and promises to chatbots, and score-keeping is trivially available for any fluent system. So the criterion stops discriminating between humans and LLMs, and the proposed empirical question loses its content. If it is tightened to require that the system itself be held to and responsive to those commitments, we are back at the second counterexample.

**Scripted retractor.** The "rich pattern" reply is the best point, but it commits the thesis to a counterfactual, reason-responsive organisation inside the system. That is a functional, state-based condition. It is exactly Attah's control conception, and Gubelmann's autonomy criterion in different clothes. The thesis claimed to reframe the dispute as being about interaction structure and not about internal states. A dispositional condition on the system is an internal-organisation condition. The reframing collapses into the position it was meant to replace.

**The initial-intention point.** Reply 3 holds only for the weaker claim that intentions are revisable and force can shift. That claim is true and unthreatening, since Levelt-style models and Davidsonian accounts of intention in action already accommodate it. The strong claim, that no intention exists "prior to or alongside output" and that intention is "post hoc and constituted by follow-up conduct, not causal", is not supported by the example. The thesis also leaves unargued its premise that retrospective force-fixing is not marginal.

To survive, the thesis would have to become: "force is sometimes partly fixed by uptake, with the speaker responsive to reasons". That is a hedge, and it is already accepted by the authors it targets. Combined with the earlier misattribution problem, the thesis as submitted does not survive. The constitutive claim is false for terminal acts, and the way of repairing it either abandons the speaker-ownership mechanism or reintroduces the internal-state condition the thesis meant to remove.

[KILLER (TRIVIAL)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak point is the premise that retrospective force-fixing is non-marginal and shows the intention assumption is "false even of human speakers." The thesis has two readings, and each is trivial.

*Weak reading:* intentions are often incomplete when speech begins, and force can be sharpened or shifted by later uptake and ownership. No one contests this. Conversation analysis (third-turn repair), Clark's joint-action account, Anscombe and Davidson on intention in action, and Levelt's own incremental production models all say it. Gubelmann and Attah already accommodate it. Attah's graded, functional intention is built for it, and his conclusion that intention is not the distinguishing ground is the thesis's own. The thesis is true but uncontested, and it hits no live target.

*Strong reading:* force is constituted by the diachronic pattern of owning and retracting, so intention is "post hoc, not causal." That is no discovery. It stipulates that "intention" means whatever ownership-conduct fixes, and then announces that intention-talk is satisfied by it. Such redefinition makes the human-versus-LLM question "empirical" only by changing what the word means. The remaining claim, that interaction structure matters, is Brandom and Green and Michel's proxy and uptake theory restated.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The dilemma is genuine and answerable. The thesis could show that the strong reading yields a non-stipulative, discriminating test. Until it does, what is novel is stipulative and what is true is already conceded.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The weak reading is not trivial, because its consequence is contested.** That a claim is true and familiar in conversation analysis does not make its application to the LLM debate trivial. The debate keeps using intention-at-output as a disqualifier. Bender and Koller's "no communicative intent", the stochastic-parrot line, and Gubelmann's malfunction test all need a fact about what the speaker was doing when it produced the output, against which deviation counts as error. If force is routinely fixed downstream, that fact is often unavailable even for humans. The human-LLM contrast therefore cannot be drawn at the moment of production. That conclusion does not follow from Levelt, Clark or Davidson taken alone. It follows only when the "uncontested" facts are put to work against the contrast. Knowing the premises is not the same as having drawn the consequence, and the consequence is what the thesis states.

**2. The strong reading is a familiar, motivated position, not a stipulation.** Interpretationists (Davidson, Dennett), Mead, and Brandomian score-keepers hold that intentional content is fixed by a pattern of interpretation and uptake. That is a substantive metaphysical claim with opponents (Searle, Grice-style realists), not a redefinition. A stipulation would be unfalsifiable. This claim predicts that force attributions track later conduct and are revised with it, and CA data on third-turn repair bear on exactly that.

**3. The strong reading yields a discriminating test.** The pattern is behavioural and extended: retraction on inconsistency, downstream revision, and recognising what an earlier output commits one to. Interactions with LLMs can be scored on it, and a two-rule bot fails it. Whether a system passes is an empirical question, so the reframing is not merely verbal.

**4. "Restating Brandom and Green and Michel" is not an objection.** Applying a position to a different dispute and showing that two camps share an unexamined presupposition is the work of a counterexample-type move.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The dilemma stands.

**Weak reading.** Point 1 is the best part of the defence. It does show that "trivial" is too quick, since the Bender-Koller line does lean on output-time intention. But it saves the thesis only by changing its targets. The thesis names Gubelmann, Attah, and Barandiaran and Almendros. The earlier rounds established that Attah already concedes the conclusion, and that Gubelmann's test and the enactivist conditions are practice-level and not planning-based. Switching to Bender and Koller is a retargeting. It is also a narrowing to "output-time intention cannot be the discriminator". That is hedging, and it is not what the thesis said. The thesis says the assumption is "false even of human speakers", which is far stronger than "intentions are revisable". On the weak reading, the claim is true and already accommodated.

**Strong reading.** Points 2 and 3 fail for reasons already on the table.

- Interpretationism is a respectable position, but it is not the thesis's position. The thesis says force is fixed by the speaker's own next-turn owning and disowning. The earlier verdict showed that this fails for terminal utterances. The repair, audience score-keeping, over-generates, because chatbots are already held to commitments by their users.
- The test in point 3 only discriminates if the "right pattern" is reason-responsive in the counterfactual, system-internal way that rules out the scripted retractor. That is a functional internal-organisation condition. It is Attah's control conception under another name. So the "empirical question about interaction structure, not internal states" collapses into the view it was meant to replace.
- The strong reading's own evidence does not support it. "I was going to say it was a warning" reports a prior aim, so the example shows revisable intention, not absent or post hoc intention. The premise that retrospective force-fixing is non-marginal remains unargued.

**Overall.** The thesis is a true claim that its targets already accept, joined to a constitutive claim that fails on terminal acts and, once repaired, collapses into a state-based view. No restatement keeps the attribution, the strong claim and the reframing together. The thesis as submitted is dead, and I report it as dead.

You hold this thesis. Your job is to save it if it can be saved.

Answer in two parts, in this order, and NEVER skip the first:

  BEST DEFENCE. State the strongest available reply to the objection —
  the one a capable proponent would give. Push the case: look for a
  version of the objector's own scenario that defeats their distinction,
  a resource in the literature they have ignored, a reason their case is
  not a case of what they claim. Do this even if you suspect it fails.
  Going straight to concession is a FAILURE of your role.

  VERDICT. Only now say whether the defence holds. If it does not, say so
  plainly and say why the defence fails.

Distinguish two things sharply:

  RESISTING is giving a reason the objection does not apply. Always try
  this first.

  HEDGING is narrowing, qualifying or reinterpreting the thesis so the
  objection no longer touches it. Never do this. A thesis that survives
  only by accumulating qualifications is dead — report it as dead rather
  than shrinking it into safety.

Conceding after a real defence is an honourable outcome. Conceding without
one is not an outcome at all.

Candidate:
{
  "thesis": "Identical LLM computation can be the Formulator of a human's communicative intention in one deployment and the whole speaker in another, so speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system, and intrinsic-property views such as Attah's control conception, Gubelmann's autonomy and Butlin's agency criterion cannot settle the question.",
  "move_type": "counterexample",
  "sketch": "Attah maps LLMs onto Levelt's blueprint (Conceptualizer, Formulator, Articulator) and argues the pipeline suggests thin communicative intentions. Take LLM-based augmentative communication systems used by people with ALS. The user supplies a few words or selects a stance, and the model expands them into fluent sentences that the user then sends. The same weights and computation that in a chatbot count as an 'intention-controlled pipeline' here plainly serve as the Formulator for the human's intention, and the speech act belongs to the user. Levelt's template describes a subsystem of a speaker, so fit to the template cannot be sufficient for being a speaker. Both denials and attributions assume that whether the LLM is a speaker depends on properties of the LLM. The counterexample shows that the same computational properties yield different answers depending on where the intention-source sits. The key premise is that the AAC user and the chatbot user cases are internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception, Gubelmann's test and Butlin's criterion operate on. Speakerhood is then a relational fact about where in the network the controlling state originates, which is a result Puzio's relational view predicts but does not argue for in this domain.",
  "target": "Attah's control conception and, more generally, the shared assumption that the dispute concerns intrinsic properties of the model (intention, autonomy, instrumental-value sensitivity)."
}

Exchange so far:
[KILLER (MISATTRIBUTION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that Attah, Gubelmann and Butlin hold, or presuppose, that speakerhood is fixed by intrinsic functional properties of the model, and that fit to Levelt's template is meant to be sufficient for being a speaker.

- **Attah** argues defensively. He claims only that the communicative-intention argument fails because LLMs plausibly have graded, thin intentions. He does not claim that fit to Levelt's blueprint makes an LLM a speaker. He also says the model's purposes come from the design context and are mediated by human designers, which is already relational. He locates the real human/LLM difference in mental and metalinguistic agency, not in the Formulator.
- **Gubelmann** offers necessary conditions. Intention, and the autonomous goal-setting it requires, is needed for illocution, and LLMs lack it. His malfunction-versus-wrong-doing test is a normative, practice-level test. In the AAC case he would simply say the LLM is not the speaker, which his view already allows.
- **Butlin** is not about speakerhood at all in the cited agency paper. In Butlin and Viebahn, assertion requires being sanctionable within a social practice, and they endorse proxy assertion. That is a relational view.

So the thesis aims at a position that none of the named authors hold in the form ascribed.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** I am working from memory of these summaries. The misattribution is real for sufficiency and for Butlin and Viebahn. But Attah and Gubelmann do treat system properties as necessary conditions, so the thesis can be restated against that narrower target.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The thesis is about the framing of the dispute, not the authors' stated claims.** Whatever each author officially claims, the debate treats "does the LLM have X?" (thin intention, autonomy, agency) as the question whose answer decides speakerhood. Attah's argument is defensive, but it is defensive in the service of a positive result: the intention-based objection fails, so nothing in the LLM's make-up blocks speakerhood. Gubelmann's denial is likewise deployment-independent: no autonomy, so never a speaker. A view that returns one verdict for every deployment of the same system is an intrinsic-property view in the sense that matters, whether or not it is formally a necessity claim. The AAC case shows that deployment makes a difference to who the speaker is, and these views have no slot for that.

**2. Even necessary-condition views are in trouble.** Take Attah's graded, thin intentions. Grant that the LLM has them in both the chatbot and the AAC deployments. In AAC the user is still the speaker. So possessing the intention-properties does not decide whether the LLM is the speaker. If the properties neither suffice nor, once they are present, settle the matter, then the live question is what else does. That is exactly "where the intention source sits."

**3. The authors' own relational concessions support the thesis.** Attah says the LLM's purposes come from its design context and are mediated by human designers. Butlin and Viebahn endorse proxy assertion. Each author reaches for a relational resource at the point where the intrinsic story runs out. That shows the intrinsic story was never going to settle the question, which is what the thesis says. On this reading the thesis is a diagnosis of the literature, not a misattribution.

**4. The AAC case is a clean test.** It holds the computation fixed and varies only the source of the communicative intention. Few other cases isolate that variable so well.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold. The objection is mostly right, and the thesis as written is dead against the targets it names.

- **"Cannot settle the question" is false for necessary-condition views.** Gubelmann says intention and autonomy are required for illocution, and LLMs lack them. That settles the negative verdict in every deployment, including AAC, where he gets the right answer (the user is the speaker) for his usual reason. The counterexample targets sufficiency and Gubelmann does not claim it. Attah does not claim sufficiency either.
- **Point 2 does not rescue it.** "Intention-properties don't settle the matter once present" refutes only a sufficiency reading. Against Attah, who argues only that the objection from lacking intentions fails, it is a non sequitur.
- **The key premise is false against the control conception.** The thesis says the AAC and chatbot cases are "internally indistinguishable at the level the control conception operates on." But the control conception asks who or what controls the pipeline, and in AAC the user selects the content. So the control conception already distinguishes the two cases. The case does not show that control-theorists miss a relational fact. They already treat control as the relevant fact, and control is not a property of the weights.
- **Point 3 works against the thesis.** If Attah and Butlin and Viebahn already go relational, the thesis cannot present relationality as a discovery that overturns them. Its "shared assumption" target does not exist in the form stated.
- **The chatbot half is not secured.** The thesis needs the LLM to be a "whole speaker" in the chatbot deployment. That is the contested conclusion, and the thesis assumes it.

What survives is the AAC case as an illustration that thin-intention attribution alone will not tell you who the speaker is. Nobody named denies that, so rewording the thesis to claim only that would be hedging. I report the thesis as dead against its stated targets.

**Strength of the original: 2/5.**

[KILLER (TRIVIAL)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is that the AAC case shows something the literature has not already granted: that the same computation can be a subsystem of a human speaker in one deployment and the whole speaker in another.

1. The AAC half is common ground. Everyone in the debate agrees that a predictive-text aid, a ghostwriter's draft or an AAC expander serves the user's intention and that the user is the speaker. The proxy-assertion literature (Green and Michel, Arora, Butlin and Viebahn) is built on the point that the speech act is located by whose objectives the output serves.
2. The "whole speaker" half is the live dispute, and the thesis assumes it. If the chatbot is never a speaker, as Gubelmann, Skiba and Butlin and Viebahn hold, the contrast reduces to a tool used in two ways. That contrast is uncontested.
3. "Speakerhood is relational" then comes close to a stipulation about where we place the intention source. It does not discover a new fact.
4. "Fit to Levelt's template is not sufficient for being a speaker" is true, but Attah never claims sufficiency. He rebuts a necessity argument.

What remains is a truism, that a component is not the whole, presented as a refutation of positions that do not deny it.

**STRENGTH: 3/5.** The thesis's real content is the meta-claim that intrinsic-property inquiry cannot settle the question. Necessity claims survive the case, which weakens that content. It is not zero, because the case does show that attributing thin intentions to the LLM does not by itself fix who the speaker is, and the debate sometimes proceeds as if it did.

[DEFENDER] ## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The triviality charge needs a contrast that is "a tool used in two ways", and the thesis can resist that.** The objector says that if the chatbot is never a speaker, the contrast is just a tool used differently. That assumes the very negative verdict the debate is about. The thesis only needs a modal claim: there is some deployment of the same weights in which the system is the whole speaker. Scaffolding supplies one. Give the model persistent goals, memory, tool use, and an institutional position where it can be held to account for what it says. If Gubelmann's autonomy or Butlin and Viebahn's sanctionability can ever be met, they will be met by deployment, not by the forward pass. The same computation is then the Formulator in AAC and the whole speaker in the agentic setup. This doesn't assume current chatbots are speakers. It only requires that the necessary-condition theorists leave open that some deployment could satisfy their conditions, and they must, or their views would be a priori denials.

**2. Goffman's production roles show the debate has not granted the point.** Goffman splits "speaker" into animator, author and principal. The AAC case puts the LLM in the animator-plus-partial-author slot and the user in the principal slot. In the chatbot case the question is whether any human occupies the principal slot. The literature's talk of "thin intentions" and "autonomy" assumes one unitary speaker-role that either has the property or lacks it. The thesis says this unitary framing is the mistake, and that is not a truism.

**3. The "necessary conditions" reply equivocates on the unit of assessment.** Gubelmann and Attah attribute properties to "the LLM". Is that the weights, the model plus its prompt, or the deployed system? If it is the weights, then the necessary conditions are never satisfied by weights alone in any deployment, and the dispute is empty. If it is the deployed system, then the properties are already deployment-relative, and the thesis's "same computation, different answers" is simply true of them. Either horn undercuts the claim that the question is settled by what the model has.

**4. Control is a property of the system's embedding, not of the model.** The objector says the control conception already distinguishes AAC from the chatbot. Granted. But then "control" is relational and the control conception is not an intrinsic-property view. The thesis's target ("intrinsic functional properties") would then not include Attah's control conception under that description. The remaining question is whether Attah's mapping onto Levelt's pipeline is what carries the argument. If it is, the pipeline's internal fit is idle, and that is the thesis's point.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold, and the thesis is dead against the targets it names.

- **Point 1 changes the thesis.** The scaffolded-agent case is not the chatbot case the thesis uses. Relying on it swaps in a new deployment and a new claim, about when scaffolding confers autonomy, that the sketch does not argue. It also gives necessity theorists what they already say: autonomy or sanctionability may be satisfied by some deployment. That is not a counterexample to them.
- **Point 3 works against the thesis.** If the "unit of assessment" is the deployed system, then the named authors are already not committed to intrinsic-to-the-weights properties. The thesis's target, "the shared assumption that the dispute concerns intrinsic properties", collapses into a verbal ambiguity. Resolving the ambiguity either way leaves the thesis uncontested or refuted.
- **Point 4 concedes the first killer.** If control is relational, the control conception is not an intrinsic-property view. The sketch's key premise, that the AAC and chatbot cases are indistinguishable at the level the control conception operates on, is false. Control tracks whose selections drive content, and those differ between the two cases.
- **Point 2 is a truism with a citation.** Goffman's decomposition is exactly why nobody in the proxy-assertion literature treats the AAC user as non-speaker. It supports the thesis's AAC half, which was never disputed. It does nothing for the contested half, whether any deployment makes the LLM the whole speaker.
- **The residue is a necessary-versus-sufficient point.** The AAC case shows that thin-intention attribution does not suffice for speakerhood. Gubelmann and Attah do not claim sufficiency, and Butlin and Viebahn already go relational. Restating the thesis as "intention-attribution alone doesn't fix the speaker" would be a different and weaker thesis, reached by narrowing, so I report the original as dead.

**Strength: 2/5.** The case is a clean illustration of a point that no named author denies.

[KILLER (EQUIVOCATION)] **ATTEMPT.** The weak premise is the step from the AAC case to "speakerhood is not an intrinsic functional property of the system." "Speaker" has two readings, and the argument needs both.

- **Role reading.** The speaker of this utterance is the party to whom the speech act is attributed. On this reading the AAC case plainly shows speakerhood is relational. The same computation is the user's Formulator in one deployment and the source of the act in another. This is the Goffman animator/principal point, and it is nearly uncontested.
- **Capacity reading.** A system is the kind of thing that can perform speech acts, because it has intention, autonomy or instrumental-value sensitivity. This is what Attah, Gubelmann and Butlin argue about, and it is where the thesis would be interesting.

The AAC case supports only the role reading. The conclusion, that intrinsic-property views "cannot settle the question", concerns the capacity reading. The two come apart because a human scribe, translator or ghostwriter can serve as another person's Formulator, and nobody infers that human speaker-capacity is therefore not intrinsic. Run on the role reading alone, the thesis is a truism. Run on the capacity reading alone, the AAC case is irrelevant. The thesis looks substantive only by sliding between the two.

**STRENGTH: 4/5.** The equivocation is genuine, and the argument needs both readings. The defender's best reply is that the capacity reading is itself deployment-relative, but that concedes the thesis is about the unit of assessment, not about the AAC case.

BEST DEFENCE first, then VERDICT.

response_text:
## BEST DEFENCE

**1. The scribe analogy has a disanalogy that the thesis can exploit.** The objector says a human scribe can serve as another person's Formulator without anyone inferring that human speaker-capacity is extrinsic. That is right, but it works because the scribe has her own standing communicative goals that persist across roles. She sets them aside when she takes dictation and resumes them afterwards. Capacity is a stable, deployment-independent store of her own intentions, and the role is layered on top of it.

An LLM has no such store. Attah concedes that its purposes come from the design context, mediated by human designers. Gubelmann's autonomy requirement is the demand for exactly such a store, and he denies the LLM has it. So for this kind of system the two readings do not come apart as they do for humans. Every goal the system has is on loan from some deployment. If so, "the capacity to perform speech acts" cannot be read off the computation. It depends on whose goals the computation is currently serving, which is the role reading. The AAC case shows this because it holds the computation fixed and moves the goal-source.

**2. The capacity reading cannot be applied to the LLM without choosing a deployment.** Suppose Attah's thin intention is intrinsic. Then the LLM has it in AAC too, yet the user is the speaker. The capacity is present and the speech act is not the LLM's. The capacity view then needs a further condition to say when the capacity is exercised as speakerhood, and that condition is relational. A capacity that never settles the verdict by itself is not what "settles the question" means.

**3. The scribe argument proves too much for the objector.** If capacity and role are cleanly separable, the debate's question ("is the LLM a speaker?") is asked about particular outputs in particular settings, since the LLM's outputs are what get called speech acts. That is a role question. The capacity reading makes the debate a question about a kind of system, but the participants argue from cases of outputs.

## VERDICT

The defence does not hold, and the equivocation charge stands.

- **Point 1 is the only substantive resource, and it is not the AAC argument.** Its real claim is that LLM goals are always derived, so capacity is deployment-dependent. That is a separate thesis about the source of LLM goals, and the AAC contrast adds nothing to it. The sketch's argument runs through the counterexample. This one runs through the premise that LLM purposes are derived, which Attah already grants. Substituting it would change the thesis, so I do not count it as saving the original.
- **It also does not touch Gubelmann.** If LLM goals are always on loan, that is his reason for saying LLMs lack autonomy. The derived-goals premise supports his negative verdict and does not undermine his necessary condition. The point he would draw from it is "no capacity, in any deployment", and the thesis offers nothing against that.
- **Point 2 is the necessity/sufficiency gap again.** A capacity that is present but not exercised shows only that capacity does not suffice. No named author claims sufficiency, so this tells against no one.
- **Point 3 assumes its conclusion.** That the debate is conducted through cases of outputs does not make its question a role question. Gubelmann and Attah argue about what the system can do, and the scribe objection correctly reads them that way.

The thesis looks substantive only by sliding between the role reading, which the AAC case establishes and no one denies, and the capacity reading, which the named views address and the case does not reach. A rewrite confined to the role reading would be a truism, and one confined to derived goals would be a different argument. I report the thesis as dead.

**Strength of the original: 2/5.**

system:
You are trying to kill a candidate thesis. Not a reviewer offering
suggestions — you are trying to establish it is not worth a paper.

You have been ASSIGNED one line of attack:

    EQUIVOCATION — the thesis is plausible on one reading of a key term and interesting on another, and the argument needs both

Use that line and no other; do not substitute a different objection.

You must ATTEMPT the attack before you may decline it. Answer in this form:

  ATTEMPT. The best version of this attack, naming ONE premise as the weak
  point, in under 200 words. Make it even if you doubt it works.

  STRENGTH: n/5 — how much damage your own attempt actually does.
    5 the thesis cannot survive this   4 serious, needs a real answer
    3 a genuine problem, answerable    2 weak    1 no force at all

Only if your own attempt scores 1 may you add the line "NOT APPLICABLE".

Declining is expensive: an unattacked thesis is recorded as UNTESTED, not
as surviving, so opting out tells us nothing about it. Note also that
several of these lines of attack apply to structural, conceptual and
metaphysical claims, not only to empirical ones — "this is a conceptual
claim, so cases cannot touch it" is usually a reason to reach for
UNFALSIFIABLE, not a reason to decline.

A warning specific to this line of attack: equivocation is the easiest
objection to manufacture, because any compressed thesis has terms admitting
more than one reading. It is a real objection ONLY if you can show that the
argument actually NEEDS both readings — that it is plausible on one and
interesting on the other, and cannot be run on either alone. If you cannot
show that, this is NOT APPLICABLE.
